extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for patent examiners on identifying, construing, documenting, and evaluating claim limitations that invoke 35 U.S.C. § 112(f) (means-plus-function and step-plus-function limitations), including adequacy of supporting disclosure for definiteness, written description, and enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine whether a claim limitation invokes § 112(f) (3‑prong analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the 3‑prong analysis in MPEP § 2181(I): (A) the claim limitation uses the term “means” or “step” or a term used as a substitute for “means” that is a generic placeholder; (B) that term is modified by functional language (typically linked by “for”, or phrases like “configured to” or “so that”); and (C) the term is not modified by sufficient structure, material, or acts for performing the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A limitation meeting all three prongs is to be interpreted under § 112(f). Use the claims, specification, and the understanding of persons of ordinary skill in the art to perform the analysis. If ambiguous, state the examiner's interpretation on the record. See MPEP § 2181(I).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumptions about use or absence of the words “means” or “step”
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limitation is presumed to invoke § 112(f) when it explicitly uses the term “means” or “step” and includes functional language. By contrast, a limitation that does not use the term “means” or “step” triggers the presumption that § 112(f) does not apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always consider whether the presumptions are overcome by claim language (e.g., use of “means” plus sufficient structure overcomes the presumption; use of a generic placeholder with functional language and lacking structure invokes §112(f)). Document any overcoming of presumptions in the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation standard for ‘sufficient structure’
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard is whether the words of the claim are understood by persons of ordinary skill in the art to have a sufficiently definite meaning as the name for structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the Williamson v. Citrix standard (quoted in MPEP § 2181). There are no absolute lists; the examiner must evaluate the term in light of the specification and the commonly accepted meaning in the technological art because claim interpretation turns on the facts of each application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms that may or may not be generic placeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain terms have been found not to be generic placeholders in some cases (e.g., “code,” “application,” “program,” “user interface code”) where POSITA would understand them as connoting structure; other terms have been found, in certain circumstances, to be structural generic placeholders invoking §112(f) (e.g., “mechanism for,” “module for,” “device for,” “unit for,” “component for,” “element for,” “member for,” “apparatus for,” “machine for,” “system for”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on fixed lists; consider examples in MPEP § 2181(I)(A) and analyze the term in context of the specification and the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability rules for step-plus-function in process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Means-plus-function limitations are common; step-plus-function limitations are rare. In process claims, use of the phrase “step for” is presumed to invoke §112(f), but the term “step” alone and the phrase “steps of” tend to show that §112(f) does not apply. A step limitation must not recite an act to be treated under §112(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most process claims include steps with acts described by verbs ending in “-ing” (e.g., passing, heating, reacting, transferring, determining), which will avoid §112(f). Structural elements may appear in both product and process claims—review all claim types for means/step plus-function issues. See MPEP § 2181(I).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory construction and claim scope when § 112(f) applies
rubrics_metrics.description: When § 112(f) applies, the claim limitation shall be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that invoking §112(f) can narrow claim scope relative to a non‑means formulation; that affects searching and prior-art application. Make the construction explicit in the record so applicants and the public understand how prior art was applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the prosecution record clear about § 112(f) interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishing the interpretation of §112(f) limitations in writing during prosecution is critical to supporting a clear prosecution record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use available form paragraphs to create a claim interpretation section in an Office action, set forth presumptions and clarifying remarks, notify the applicant/public/courts how the claim was construed, and allow early clarification by the applicant so the examiner can revisit prior art if needed. See MPEP § 2181(VI).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness under § 112(b) for § 112(f) limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The corresponding structure must be disclosed in the specification itself in a way that one skilled in the art will understand what structure will perform the entire recited function; otherwise the claim fails §112(b) and is indefinite. The disclosed structure must be clearly linked or associated with the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definiteness is distinct from enablement; if no disclosure of structure for performing the entire recited function exists, find the claim indefinite. Indefiniteness based solely on an inconclusive 3‑prong analysis should be rare because examiners should be able to determine whether claim words recite structure using the claims, specification, and knowledge of POSITA. When ambiguous, state interpretation on the record. See MPEP § 2181(II) and following.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special considerations for computer-implemented § 112(f) limitations (algorithm requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: For computer-implemented §112(f) claim limitations, the specification must disclose an algorithm for performing the claimed specific computer function, or the claim should be found indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The algorithm may be expressed in any understandable terms (mathematical formula, prose, flow chart, etc.). A disclosure that only identifies a general-purpose computer as the structure for performing a specific function is inadequate to satisfy §112(b). Assess sufficiency in light of the level of ordinary skill in the art. See MPEP § 2181(II)(B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate written description and enablement under § 112(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: A §112(f) limitation that is indefinite under §112(b) for lack of disclosed corresponding structure will also lack adequate written description and may not be sufficiently enabled to support the full scope of the claim under §112(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the specification describes the claimed invention in sufficient detail to show possession as of the filing date and whether the disclosure contains sufficient information for a person skilled in the art to make and use the invention. See MPEP § 2181(IV) and § 2185.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use MPEP §§ 2181–2187 and available USPTO training resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should refer to MPEP sections 2181–2187 for guidance on determining invocation of §112(f), making the record clear, and evaluating supporting disclosure under §§112(a) and (b). Refresher training (computer-based and instructor-led) is available through the Office of Patent Training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific training modules include: “Examining Computer‑Implemented Functional Claim Limitations for Compliance with 35 U.S.C. § 112,” “Application of New Form Paragraphs for Addressing Issues Related to §112(f) or ‘Means‑plus‑Function’ Limitations,” and “Addressing 35 U.S.C. §112(f) or ‘Means‑plus‑Function’ Limitations in an Office Action using New Form Paragraphs.” Technology Center points of contact and intranet resources are available.
